title: Australians reject retirement stereotypes as pressures mount
full_text:
Just one in nine HESTA members, or 11 per cent, believed media portrayals of retirement reflected the future they saw for themselves, according to a survey released by the fund.
The findings have prompted HESTA to call for changes to modernise Australia’s retirement system, including removing barriers that discourage pensioners from working and allowing super funds to guide members towards suitable retirement products.
HESTA chief experience officer Lisa Samuels said Australians were looking for greater support to shape their retirement around their individual circumstances.
“There is clearly a significant gap between the stock image of retirement and the reality most Australians are [facing]. Retirement is different for everyone and Australians are looking for support to retire their way,” Samuels said.
“More than 2.5 million Australians are expected to retire over the next decade and right now, many are just focused on getting through next week. And for those beyond retirement age, we are seeing large numbers of people wanting to return to work later in their lives to support their finances or retain connection to their communities.
“It’s in this environment that we need to look at further ways to modernise the system so that it can help more Australians retire the way they want to. These proposed reforms range from practical fixes for pensioners in the workforce to new powers for funds to guide members into suitable retirement products at the right moment.”
Cost-of-living pressures have also disrupted retirement planning, with one-third of respondents reporting that higher expenses had affected their ability to manage their super.
Members surveyed wanted to retire at an average age of 66, one year before becoming eligible for the Age Pension but six years after they could begin accessing their super savings.
The responses suggested work remained part of the retirement outlook for many members, alongside concerns about whether they would be financially comfortable.
“When we asked members for words that come to mind when thinking about their future retirement, the most common weren’t ‘cruises’, ‘golf’, ‘travel’ or even ‘relaxed’. Instead, leading the way were ‘comfortable’, ‘time’, ‘happy’, and ‘work’, alongside several references to feeling ‘anxious’. This is the real life experience many Australians expect,” Samuels said.
HESTA called for employment income to be removed from the Age Pension Income Test, arguing pensioners should be able to work more while retaining more of their earnings.
The fund also proposed allowing super funds to prompt members towards specific retirement products when they were ready to move into the retirement phase.
Other proposed changes included enabling members to add employment earnings to their retirement income streams and establishing data-sharing arrangements between funds and government agencies.
HESTA said greater access to data could support improved advice, member engagement and retirement services.
